# Build: Turn the Design Into a Working System

:::{.callout-important}
## In Brief
Build turns the locked Design Brief into a working, deployed system. It makes one thing, the eight-section Build Spec, and runs that spec through three gates: audit the spec before anyone builds, answer the seven guardrails questions before it touches live work, run the Done Test before you hand off. Build is also where you pick the specific product the workflow runs on, inside the category you chose in Design. Build is done when the system handles real inputs in production and the named Human Orchestrator can review what it produces. If Build feels chaotic, the problem is upstream.
:::

Sofia read every agent output to start, working off the daily review task the coordination agent created for her each morning. The agents drafted; she reviewed. When a client's timeline slipped and somebody had to decide whether to tell them that day or wait for the Friday update, that call stayed with her. It always had. What changed was that she no longer spent her mornings chasing task updates to find out the timeline had slipped at all.

We had built her a team of five agents to replace a $24,000-a-year coordinator role. One created tasks from project charters. One assigned the day's work and flagged conflicts. One wrote the variance reports. One sent people their own overdue and blocked items in Slack. One scanned for bad data: missing estimates, half-written descriptions, projects nobody had defined properly.

We locked the Hybrid Accountability Chart entry before we built a single workflow step. Sofia as Human Orchestrator, every agent starting AI-Assisted, her sign-off on every output in Sprint one. Every access boundary came out of that one call. The task-creation agent could read and write in our project management system, and everything it produced posted to Slack for review, never to a client. The one pulling billable hours and delivery pace could see numbers we don't show clients, and nothing client-facing. The data-quality scanner touched neither: task fields only, no financials and nothing a client would ever see. Same team, five different sets of keys, and we cut every key before anyone built anything.

## Build ships one *deployed* system.

Build is the most variable stage in the Sequence. The problem, the systems, the team's technical comfort, and the data all shape what it looks like in practice. The constant is what it ships: a working, deployed system aimed at the constraint you validated in Signal.

*Working* means it produces outputs the Human Orchestrator can review and trust, judged the way they'd judge a person's work.

*Deployed* means it runs inside the actual business, wired to the systems it needs, putting what it produces where the work already lives.

Build stops there. Briefing the team, changing the handoffs around the new workflow, retiring the old way: that's Deliver. What Build owes Deliver is the list of every person whose day changes when this goes live.

The most common way a Build goes wrong is scope drift, and it usually isn't the builder who drifts. It's the process owner. The person who scoped the workflow watches it take shape, their eyes get bigger, and they want more than they scoped. Another feature, a second system connected, and eventually the whole workflow generalized into a platform. A locked Design Brief leaves little to renegotiate, so this mostly doesn't come up. When it does, the ask goes on the Constraint Backlog and waits for the next Sprint. It's a different project.

Build what the design calls for and nothing more elaborate. A bigger build than the design asked for is scope drift on the builder's side of the table.

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
The time box doesn't move. That leaves scope as the only variable you actually control, so when a build runs long, cut what the workflow does. Ship the version that handles the inputs you see most often and put the rest on the Constraint Backlog for the next Sprint. A deployed system that handles the common case earns money while it waits.
:::

The other thing that stalls a build mid-stream is a design gap: a call that belonged in Design, never got made there, and surfaces now, where it costs more to settle. Two moves. If the gap makes it impossible to finish the build correctly, stop, go back to Design, fix it, resume. Otherwise log it for the next Sprint's Signal session, with enough context to pick it up later. Don't absorb an unlogged gap into the build. That turns a defined gap into an invisible one.

## The builder is the person closest to the *work*.

Most teams we've run Sprints with assume Build means hand it to engineering. Then the Sprint waits. The developer is three projects deep, and the constraint keeps costing what it costs.

Build doesn't require developers. Not always, not on every path. What it requires is curiosity and systems thinking. Jesse teaches psychology, economics, and criminal justice majors at Michigan State, not engineers or computer scientists. Within a semester those students are building working data pipelines: pulling data from APIs, running it through agents, writing the results back. That's the bar. A computer science degree isn't.

Anyone on your team who's smart and diligent can learn to build a skill, which is one packaged capability an agent runs: an instruction set plus the reference material it works from. Claude's project interface gets you a working skill inside a conversation. Replit lets a non-developer ship a working app by describing what they want. n8n, the low-code platform from Source, connects systems by dragging and linking blocks instead of writing code.

The developer-free claim covers the design and setup work in this book. When the workflow needs systems wired to each other, you may have to buy a few days of somebody else's time. Section 8 is where that gets named and budgeted.

### What IT owns: the keys, not the build.

IT controls the keys: who gets into which system, under which policy, with which credentials. When Build needs a CRM connection or ERP read access, IT gates it. IT doesn't need to prototype the workflow or write the skill. The person closest to the work builds it; IT makes sure it's safe. No IT department? You hold the keys, and the same split holds.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Before your next Build, ask one question: does the builder need to be a developer, or does the builder need to be the person who knows the work? If it's the second, expect them to spend part of the time box learning the tool, and pair them with whoever controls access and security rather than with someone you expect to do the building.
:::

## One document, three *gates*.

Build makes one document and runs it through three gates. Every numbered list in this chapter belongs to one of them.

1. **Write the Build Spec.** Eight sections. Four you copy forward from Design; four you decide here.
2. **Gate 1 — audit the spec.** Seven checks, before anyone starts building.
3. **Build it.**
4. **Gate 2 — answer the guardrails questions.** Seven answers in writing, before it touches live work.
5. **Gate 3 — run the Done Test.** Five questions against last week's real inputs, before you hand off.

The three gates look alike on the page. They aren't. Each one tests a different thing, at a different moment.

| | What it tests | When you run it | What it asks |
|---|---|---|---|
| **The Build Spec** | the work | before anything | What are we building? |
| **Gate 1 — spec audit** | *the document* | before you build | Is the spec good enough to hand over? |
| **Gate 2 — Guardrails Checklist** | *the permissions* | before it touches live work | Is it allowed to do this? |
| **Gate 3 — Done Test** | *the built system* | before you hand to Deliver | Does it actually work? |

{{< excalidraw ch07-build-sequence "One document, three gates: the Build Spec written from the Design Brief, then Gate 1 on the document, the build, Gate 2 on the permissions, Gate 3 on the built system, and the handoff to Deliver." >}}

The spec, the guardrails answers, and the test results fill in the Build row of your Sprint Planning Canvas and go forward to Deliver.

## Write the Build *Spec*.

The Design Brief tells you what to build. The Build Spec tells a builder how to start. Four of its eight sections say the same things in more detail: the workflow, the inputs, the outputs, the systems. You decide the other four here: what the agent may decide, who reviews its work, what happens when something breaks, and where it runs.

Neither document reopens the design conversation, and on any disagreement between them, the Design Brief wins.

<!-- moves:write-build-spec -->
### How to write the eight-section Build *Spec*

1. **Section 1: Write the workflow summary** — Gives any builder a plain-language end-to-end picture of what they're building before they touch anything.
2. **Section 2: Define the inputs** — Specifies exactly what triggers the workflow and what data enters it, so the builder knows where to reach and how to access it.
3. **Section 3: Define the outputs** — Locks the deliverable form, destination, and recipient so the build can't drift toward something the Human Orchestrator can't use.
4. **Section 4: Set agent scope boundaries** — States what the agent handles and what it cannot decide, preventing over-prescription that kills agent effectiveness.
5. **Section 5: Name the Human Orchestrator role** — Identifies who reviews, what they review for, and what the handoff looks like — the accountability anchor for the whole build.
6. **Section 6: List every system and integration** — Documents read/write access, authentication method, and data sensitivity for every system touched so nothing is wired by assumption.
7. **Section 7: Document the failure modes** — Pre-decides what happens on every edge case and outage so the builder wires escalation paths instead of improvising them under pressure.
8. **Section 8: Specify the environment and constraints** — Locks which specific platform within Design's category the build runs on and any data residency, license, or security constraints.
<!-- /moves:write-build-spec -->

Here's the blank template. Every row gets content before the spec goes to a builder. An empty row is a decision the builder ends up making instead of you.

| Section | Your Sprint |
|---|---|
| **1. Workflow summary** | _(one plain-language paragraph, end to end)_ |
| **2. Inputs** | _(trigger, data, form, source systems, access)_ |
| **3. Outputs** | _(what it produces, what form, where, to whom)_ |
| **4. Agent scope** | _(handles what; may not decide what)_ |
| **5. Human Orchestrator role** | _(who reviews, for what, where the output lands)_ |
| **6. Systems and integrations** | _(each system, read or write, auth, sensitivity)_ |
| **7. Failure modes** | _(each failure: what happens, who gets it, when)_ |
| **8. Environment and constraints** | _(the specific product, plus residency, license, security limits)_ |

The worksheet walks the fill-in row by row. The judgment isn't spread evenly: four sections you copy forward, four you decide.

### Sections 1–3 and 6: restated at builder *precision*.

The workflow summary, the inputs, the outputs, and the systems list carry no new decisions. You made those in Design. What changes is the grain. The Design Brief says the workflow pulls customer history from the CRM. The spec names the system, the fields, the access level, and how the builder signs in. A builder needs that grain to work without asking. The Design Brief never did.

If you can't reach one of those details from your Design artifacts, you've found a design gap. Go get it before the spec ships.

{{< excalidraw ch07-build-spec-progressive-1 "restated from the Design Brief — the Design Brief wins on conflict." >}}

### Section 4: agent scope is *boundaries*, not procedure.

The first section Build authors. Prescribe every step and the agent loses the flexibility that made it worth deploying. State no limits and it wanders into calls nobody gave it. A good Section 4 names what each agent handles, then draws the hard lines: the short list of things no agent may decide.

The lines follow the same shape across functions.

- A quoting agent can price against the rate card; it can't set a final price or send anything to a customer.
- A collections agent can draft reminders and flag overdue accounts; it can't change payment terms.
- A hiring agent can screen resumes against written criteria and schedule interviews; it can't reject a candidate or extend an offer.
- A support agent can answer from the documented knowledge base; it can't issue refunds or make policy exceptions.

Anything irreversible, customer-facing, or precedent-setting sits outside agent scope in the first Sprint. You can loosen a boundary later, once the quality data says so. You can't unsend a bad quote.

### Section 5: the Human Orchestrator's *working day*.

The Hybrid Accountability Chart already names the person. This section adds the shape of their day: what they check, and where the work they don't approve goes instead.

The judgment call is how specific you get. "The ops manager reviews the output" isn't a spec. Nobody can wire a review queue from it.

What a good answer looks like, across functions:

- Operations: the ops manager checks each generated work order for crew assignment and materials; anything unusual goes to the scheduler.
- Finance: the controller works flagged mismatches daily, inside the accounting system's existing exceptions view; anything over $5K goes up the same day.
- Marketing: the marketing lead reads drafted campaign copy in the approval doc the team already uses; brand-risk items route to the CEO.

{{< excalidraw ch07-build-spec-progressive-2 "the accountability layer — sections 4 and 5 written, 7 and 8 still open" >}}

### Section 7: pre-decide the *failure* modes.

The section builders need most and operators skip most. The happy path writes itself. The spec earns its keep on the inputs nobody wants to think about.

Most failure lists we've written draw on the same handful of families:

- missing data
- an input the agent doesn't recognize
- a system that's down
- output the agent isn't sure about
- a result outside the expected range

Walk each one and write down what the agent does, where the case goes, and what the flag says.

- An invoicing workflow: a PO number that matches nothing goes to the AR clerk flagged "no match found." The agent never guesses the account.
- A scheduling workflow: when the calendar system is down, requests queue. Nothing double-books.
- A content workflow: any claim the agent can't source from the approved library gets flagged, not published.

Name it, flag it, route it. The agent never guesses and never goes silent. If you can't decide where a failure goes, you've found a design gap. Don't leave it blank for the builder.

### Enough *technology* to make Section 8's call.

Section 8 asks where the workflow runs. You can't answer that, or argue with a vendor about it, without a working vocabulary for what you're buying. That's what this section is for: enough of the words to make good calls about the tools, the costs, and the trade-offs. You aren't going to out-configure your builder. You do need to know what each choice costs you.

**Models and providers.** A model is the engine. A provider is the company that built and hosts it. Right now that's Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI (GPT), Google (Gemini), Meta (Llama, open source), and smaller players like Groq and DeepSeek competing on speed or price. Each one trades something away: Claude is strong at reasoning and tool use, GPT is widely adopted with a large ecosystem around it, DeepSeek is cheap and where its data goes matters if you have rules about that. You aren't signing a five-year vendor contract. You pick the model that fits the task in your spec, and plenty of builds use one provider for drafting and a cheaper one for sorting.

**Tokens and what they cost.** Tokens, the ones you met in Source, are to AI what minutes are to a phone plan. What the model writes back costs more per token than what you send in. A workflow that reads 500 documents a day at 2,000 tokens each burns a million tokens a day. On a mid-tier model that's a rounding error. At top-tier pricing it's a line item somebody has to approve. Jesse learned that the hard way: our Anthropic bill hit four figures in a matter of days when we first started building production workflows, because nobody was watching the meter.

The fix is boring. Use the most capable model where judgment matters and a cheaper, faster one where it doesn't: sorting, summarizing, routing. Your Section 4 scope lines already tell you which is which.

**Getting the model to your data.** Three approaches, in the order to try them.

*Load it in.* Put the documents in the conversation. Nothing to build, nothing to index. This works while the material fits inside the model's context window, and it gets less reliable as you crowd that limit.

*RAG.* The retrieve-on-demand approach from Design. Cheap to keep current, because you change the reference material and not the model. It does need an indexed store and a retrieval layer somebody maintains.

*Fine-tuning.* You retrain the model on your own data so it behaves differently by default. Expensive, slow to stand up, and painful to keep current: new data means retraining. When a vendor proposes it, ask whether you'd get the same result by giving the model your data at the moment it runs. If yes, skip the fine-tune.

Start with what fits in the window, move to RAG when the data outgrows it or changes often, and fine-tune last. Your quoting agent needs a general-purpose model with reach into your historical quotes and rate card, and the Knowledge Map from Source already says where those live.

{{< excalidraw ch07-data-access-approaches "Three approaches to AI data access: context window, RAG, and fine-tuning — with trade-offs and when to use each" >}}

**One question decides more than the others: can the data leave your systems?** Proprietary models, meaning Claude, GPT, and Gemini, run on the provider's servers. Most capable, nothing for you to maintain, and your data passes through somebody else's system under their terms. Read those terms rather than assuming them; what a provider may do with your data depends on the plan you're on. Open-source models like Llama can run on hardware you control instead: the data stays home, there's no per-token bill, and somebody on your side hosts and patches them. Most Compound Sprints belong on the proprietary path. If a regulation, a contract, or your own policy says the data can't leave, that's the answer that forces open source onto your own hardware, and the same answer forces a custom server in Section 8. Settle it once, here.

### Section 8: where it *runs*, and what must be true first.

You picked one of three categories in Design: off-the-shelf, low-code, or hand-built. In Build you pick the specific product inside that category. Products change faster than the logic for picking them, so what follows is the logic. Check the market when you run your Sprint, not when you read this. Off-the-shelf points at Claude Projects or Claude Team, low-code at n8n, Make, Zapier and their peers, hand-built at Claude Code or a server of your own.

| Product | Fits | Doesn't fit | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Claude Projects** | One agent per project, one knowledge base, one Human Orchestrator; set up in an afternoon | Agents that must run at the same time, or anything programmatic | A single drafting agent working from one library |
| **Claude Team** | Cross-team, AI-assisted work where several people share the same agent context | Workflows that start themselves on a schedule | Meridian's Quote Agent Team: three projects in one workspace |
| **Claude Code** | Multi-agent, programmatic, tooling-heavy builds with triggers and write-back | Single-agent skill work that needs no infrastructure | Sofia's PM agent team, built with Claude Code and running on its own server |
| **n8n, Make, Zapier** | Data pipelines: pull, run through an agent, write back, notify | Complex branching or large volumes of unstructured data | Meridian's n8n connectors |
| **Custom server** | Data that can't leave your systems, extreme volume, or a proprietary system-of-record API | Anything a hosted or low-code path already handles | Forced by residency, volume, or reliability, never by taste |

One rule belongs to the surface rather than the product. A surface is where you actually work with a product: a website, a desktop app, a command line. On the claude.ai web surface, one project holds one running process, so running several agents there means several projects, several tabs, and one person reading all of them. The marketing lead from the Co-Operating Model chapter works that way, though not all of it inside Claude: four tools, four tabs, her as the single read on all of it. Four streams can run at once that way, as long as she supervises each one separately. What outgrows the web surface is agents that have to coordinate with each other, or a workflow that starts itself on a schedule or a trigger. Off the web, a single workspace runs several agents at once: Cowork, which is Anthropic's desktop agent workspace, or a server, or Claude Code.

Three questions route the pick inside your category.

1. Does more than one agent run under one Human Orchestrator, and do they have to run at the same time?
2. Does the workflow start itself, on a schedule or a trigger?
3. Can the data leave your systems?

Pick the least infrastructure that satisfies all three answers.

Count the agents while you're here. Past three concurrent agents under one Human Orchestrator, productivity inverts. That's the span-of-control check from Designing the Work, where Julie Bedard and colleagues at BCG report it in *Harvard Business Review*. Four or more agents under one person is a design gap, and no product choice fixes it. Either go back to Design, or give the team a coordinating agent and let the Human Orchestrator read what the coordinator surfaces instead of every agent's output.

{{< excalidraw ch07-category-to-environment "Category to environment: Design's three categories bin into five products, Meridian's low-code + off-the-shelf pick marked, routed by three questions." >}}

Then the prerequisites, which are what actually stall builds: the things that have to be true before the build starts.

- The pricing spreadsheet has to be cleaned and validated before anything gets wired to it.
- The CRM's duplicate records have to be merged before an agent starts matching against them.
- IT has to issue API credentials before the builder's clock starts, not during it.

Anything the builder would have to stop and wait for is a prerequisite. Name it with an owner and a date, or watch it eat the build from the inside.

{{< excalidraw ch07-build-spec-progressive-3 "Build Spec, stage 3 of 3: all eight sections filled, failure modes and environment now locked — the production layer." >}}

### When you need a builder you don't *have*.

Two of the three categories your team can own outright. The third is where Designing the Work told you a builder or a contractor comes in: hand-built work, or any workflow that needs systems wired to each other. Build is where you actually do it.

What you're buying is narrow. A defined wiring task against a locked spec, not discovery and not advice about what to build. The spec is what makes that safe, and this is where it earns its keep for you: a stranger who knows nothing about your business can wire your quoting workflow, because every call they'd otherwise have to invent is already written down.

Finding one is the honest gap in this chapter; we don't have a vetted sourcing playbook to hand you. Where we start: the implementation partner list from the vendor whose product you picked, and peers who've built something similar. Then use the spec itself as the interview. A builder who reads it and asks sharp questions about Sections 7 and 8 is the one to hire.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Open a document. Write the eight section headers. Fill in Sections 1–3 and 6 from your Design artifacts; if you can't fill them without guessing, Design isn't done. Then work Sections 4, 5, 7, and 8 from the Hybrid Accountability Chart and the Knowledge Map. Every section carries content before the spec goes to a builder.
:::

## Meridian's Build Spec, section by *section*.

Here's what the eight sections looked like filled in for Meridian Manufacturing, against the $558K quoting constraint.

**Section 1, Workflow summary.** An RFQ arrives through the standard intake form, creates a CRM record, and starts the workflow. The Quote Research Agent pulls customer history and matches the RFQ against three years of jobs in the ERP. The Quote Pricing Agent applies the rate card, the senior engineer's labor estimate, and whichever exception rules apply. The Quote Assembly Agent formats the draft as a PDF and drops it in Elena's review queue. She reviews it, edits, approves, and it goes to Ty, the sales lead, who sends it to the customer.

**Section 2, Inputs.** The trigger is an inbound RFQ, submitted through the standard intake form and parsed into HubSpot as a new deal record. It reads from:

- ERP job costing history (three years, roughly 800 completed jobs)
- the current rate card, which finance maintains in JobBOSS
- the cleaned pricing exceptions database (112 validated customer-specific rules)
- the senior engineer's labor hour estimate, submitted through a structured form
- CRM customer history, including win/loss records

**Section 3, Outputs.** A draft PDF quote in Meridian's standard format, landing in Elena's CRM review queue. It carries:

- a line-item breakdown: materials, labor, overhead, margin
- a confidence score, high/medium/low, which is the agent's own read on how sure it is
- the closest historical job matches, with their pricing
- every exception rule it applied
- a flag on any input it couldn't resolve

**Section 4, Agent scope.** Quote Research matches the RFQ to historical jobs by spec, materials, and complexity, then surfaces customer context and pricing terms. Quote Pricing calculates the draft price. Quote Assembly generates the PDF. No agent sets a final price, overrides the rate card, applies an undocumented exception, or sends anything to a customer.

**Section 5, Human Orchestrator.** Elena reviews every draft quote. She checks that the agent read the scope right, priced it right, scored its own confidence honestly, and applied the right exception rules. Low-confidence quotes she reworks herself. Non-standard materials go to Dave, the senior engineer; strategic-account pricing goes to Mark, the CEO.

**Section 6, Systems.**

- HubSpot CRM (read/write: customer records, RFQ intake, quote pipeline, delivery queue)
- JobBOSS ERP (read: historical job costing, rate card, materials pricing)
- Claude Team workspace (three projects, one per agent)
- n8n (connectors, moving work between the three projects)

Pricing data is medium sensitivity. Everything else is low.

Four systems and three agents in a bullet list won't show you how work moves between them. A swim lane will. You drew this workflow's swim lane in Design, before the agents existed. This is the same diagram with them in it.

{{< excalidraw ch07-meridian-swim-lane "Meridian's built quoting workflow as a swim lane: lanes for Ty in sales, the three quote agents, the CRM and ERP, and Elena as Human Orchestrator, with every handoff marked." >}}

If you want to redraw yours, the diagramming primer in the appendices walks the conventions using this same Meridian workflow as its worked example.

**Section 7, Failure modes.**

- No similar historical jobs found: flag it "insufficient for rapid estimate" and route to Elena for full manual review.
- Unknown material, titanium for instance: no price on that line item, flagged "manual pricing required."
- ERP API down: RFQs queue in the CRM and the agent works them when the connection comes back.
- Confidence below 60%: the draft goes to Elena with a warning flag.
- Price more than 15% off the closest historical match: the agent flags the gap and Elena investigates before approving.

**Section 8, Environment and constraints.** Low-code, run on n8n against an existing license, alongside Claude Team. Three days of freelance n8n work to wire HubSpot and JobBOSS. All data stays in existing systems. One prerequisite: the pricing exceptions spreadsheet gets cleaned and validated before the build clock starts.

No ambiguity meetings, no design calls made at the keyboard.

## Gate 1: Audit the spec before anyone *builds*.

The spec is written. Now test the document rather than the workflow: is it good enough to hand to somebody who doesn't know your business? Seven checks.

<!-- moves:audit-spec-failures -->
### How to audit the spec against seven common *failures*

1. **Check 1: Search for existing capabilities before building** — Prevents rebuilding what already exists — the most common implementation failure, which is a research gap, not a technical one.
2. **Check 2: Confirm the environment matches Design's category** — Stops a builder from substituting a 'cleaner' architecture for the one the spec actually calls for.
3. **Check 3: Verify the spec is complete before build starts** — Every empty section becomes an on-the-fly decision that won't match Design's intent.
4. **Check 4: Confirm the output lands where the work already lives** — A workflow that outputs to a tool no one opens produces zero adoption regardless of technical quality.
5. **Check 5: Verify Section 7 (failure modes) is populated** — A build that only handles the happy path breaks on the first edge case.
6. **Check 6: Confirm the build handles real-world edge cases, not just the demo path** — A demo shows the happy path; the build must handle missing data, system outages, and off-script inputs.
7. **Check 7: Require testing against real inputs before declaring done** — Synthetic and cherry-picked examples are not tests; last week's actual data is the only honest gate.
<!-- /moves:audit-spec-failures -->

Only the first one is new work.

**Check 1, existing capabilities.** Before anything gets built, find out whether the product you picked already does it. We've watched a team wire document search into an agent when the product they built it on already searched uploaded files out of the box. Another rebuilt a CRM connector their low-code platform ships as standard. So read the product's connector list, its docs, and its template gallery against what your spec asks for, and build only what's genuinely missing.

The other six checks re-ask something the spec already answered. That's what they're for. They read the document back against itself, section by section.

| Check | Where the answer lives | What a fail looks like |
|---|---|---|
| **2.** Environment matches the category | Section 8 | The spec says low-code and the builder proposes a custom-coded service because it's "cleaner." That disagreement goes back to Design, not to the keyboard. |
| **3.** Spec is complete | all eight sections | A blank row. Mechanical, non-negotiable: walk all eight and confirm real content in each. |
| **4.** Output lands where the work already lives | Section 3 | The output goes to a tool nobody opens. Meridian passed this one: the drafts landed in the CRM review queue Elena already worked from. |
| **5.** Failure modes populated | Section 7 | Section 7 names no edge cases, which means nobody looked. |
| **6.** Real edge cases, not the demo path | Section 7 | The spec covers the happy path and goes quiet on outages, missing data, and the Human Orchestrator on vacation. |
| **7.** Real inputs as the done gate | Gate 3, the Done Test | Nobody agreed up front what "done" gets tested against, which leaves room to declare done on a demo. |

Elena walked the seven with the freelancer before his clock started. Check 1 paid for the whole exercise: n8n's standard HubSpot connector already did what the spec asked, so nobody wrote one. JobBOSS was the real wiring job, and that's what the freelancer's three days were budgeted for. Check 3 caught the one gap that mattered. The pricing exceptions spreadsheet wasn't clean, and the audit turned a mid-build surprise into a named prerequisite with Elena's name on it. Everything else cleared.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Walk all seven checks with the builder in the room, against the finished spec. Any check you can't mark off is a gap to close before the build starts.
:::

## Gate 2: Answer the guardrails questions before it goes *live*.

The spec says what gets built. The Guardrails Checklist says what it's allowed to do once it's running, and you've already made six of these seven calls. In Design you set five: what data the agent touches, what it may do on its own, who it escalates to, how you'd measure whether it's any good, and what shuts it off. You named the sixth on the Hybrid Accountability Chart: who owns a bad output. Build adds one, and it's the hardest one to answer in the abstract: what the agent does with an input nobody designed for, at the fidelity of real production traffic.

Write all seven down anyway. A call you made in a design session and never wrote down is a call the build makes for you, differently. If you can't write one, you're not ready to go live.

{{< excalidraw ch07-guardrails-derivation "Where the seven guardrails answers come from: five from the Design Brief, one from the Hybrid Accountability Chart, one authored in Build." >}}

<!-- moves:guardrails-checklist -->
### How to answer the seven *guardrails* questions in writing

1. **Question 1: Lock data access boundaries in writing** — Documents exactly what data the system may touch and what is off-limits, with an owner for that decision.
2. **Question 2: Define agent autonomy vs. human sign-off** — Draws the exact line between what the agent can do unilaterally and what requires a human approval before action.
3. **Question 3: Specify behavior on unrecognized inputs** — Prevents the agent from guessing or going silent when it encounters something outside its design envelope.
4. **Question 4: Define quality measurement and baseline** — Makes 'good enough' measurable so the Human Orchestrator can calibrate review cadence and know when to trust the system more.
5. **Question 5: Name the escalation path** — Routes judgment-requiring outputs to a specific person, in a specific form, on a specific timeline — no ambiguity in the moment.
6. **Question 6: Name the accountability owner** — Establishes who owns a bad output the same way they'd own it if a person produced it — no diffuse responsibility.
7. **Question 7: Define the kill switch condition** — Pre-decides the specific failures that trigger immediate shutdown, so the decision isn't made under pressure after something goes wrong.
<!-- /moves:guardrails-checklist -->

| Question | Your answer |
|---|---|
| **1. Data access.** What data is the system permitted to touch? What is explicitly off-limits? Who decided, and where is it documented? |  |
| **2. Agent autonomy.** What can the agent do without human approval? What requires human sign-off? |  |
| **3. Unrecognized inputs.** When the agent encounters an input it was not designed for, what does it do? |  |
| **4. Quality measurement.** What specific checks, against what baseline, measured how? |  |
| **5. Escalation path.** When the agent produces output that requires human judgment, who does it go to? In what form? On what timeline? |  |
| **6. Accountability.** Who is responsible when the agent produces a bad output? |  |
| **7. Kill switch.** What would cause you to shut down the agent workflow immediately? |  |

### Meridian's guardrails, in *writing*.

Elena answered all seven before the build started, and most took ten minutes. She'd made the calls in Design; the checklist turned them into written commitments.

| Question | Meridian's answer |
|---|---|
| **1. Data access.** What data is the system permitted to touch? What is explicitly off-limits? Who decided, and where is it documented? | HubSpot CRM deal records (read/write), JobBOSS ERP job costing and rate card (read), cleaned pricing exceptions database (read). Off-limits: financial reporting, employee records, customer payment history, supplier contracts, or any system not listed. |
| **2. Agent autonomy.** What can the agent do without human approval? What requires human sign-off? | Can match RFQs to historical jobs, apply rate card pricing, apply documented exception rules, generate draft PDFs, assign confidence scores, place drafts in review queue. Cannot send anything to a customer, apply undocumented exceptions, override the rate card, or commit a quote. |
| **3. Unrecognized inputs.** When the agent encounters an input it wasn't designed for, what does it do? | If the RFQ references a material not in the pricing exceptions database or ERP materials list, specialty alloys like titanium, the agent produces no price estimate for that line item, flags it as "manual pricing required," and routes to the senior engineer. If the RFQ lacks sufficient spec detail, the agent flags it as "insufficient for rapid estimate" and routes to Elena. |
| **4. Quality measurement.** What specific checks, against what baseline, measured how? | Weekly comparison of agent-drafted prices to Elena's final approved prices. Target: substantive corrections on fewer than 10% of drafts within eight weeks. Historical match accuracy tracked separately, target 95% before Elena reduces review cadence on the Research Agent. |
| **5. Escalation path.** When the agent produces output that requires human judgment, who does it go to? In what form? On what timeline? | Low-confidence quotes to Elena for full manual review. Non-standard materials to Dave Kowalski (senior engineer). Strategic account pricing to Mark Ellison (CEO). Any quote where the calculated price deviates more than 15% from the closest historical match gets flagged for Elena's investigation before approval. |
| **6. Accountability.** Who is responsible when the agent produces a bad output? | Elena Ruiz, VP of Operations, owns every quote the agents produce, the same way she'd own it if she'd built it from scratch. She is the named Human Orchestrator in the Hybrid Accountability Chart. |
| **7. Kill switch.** What would cause you to shut down the agent workflow immediately? | Pricing errors exceeding 20% on three quotes in any week, any quote reaching a customer without Elena's review, or any data access outside defined scope. Elena holds the switch. |

Question 4 is the one you calibrate rather than decide. Name the check and the baseline now, the way Elena did, and expect the thresholds to move once real work runs through the system. The pilot in Deliver is where they settle. Write your best answer and plan to tune it.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Answer all seven in writing and attach the answers to the Build Spec. Any question you can't answer is a gap to close before the workflow goes live.
:::

## Gate 3: Run the Done Test before you hand off to *Deliver*.

Pull the last week of real inputs the workflow was supposed to handle, run them through the build, and answer five questions.

1. **Did it produce the expected outputs?** Compare what the agent produced against what a competent person would have produced. Not identical. Inside the range the Human Orchestrator would accept from a team member.
2. **Did it handle the edge cases?** Every failure mode you named in Section 7: did the build do what the spec said?
3. **Did it escalate correctly?** Feed it inputs that should escalate. Did the right person get it, in the right form, on the right timeline?
4. **Could the Human Orchestrator read the output without a walkthrough?** Hand it over with no explanation. Can they evaluate it and decide?
5. **Is the handoff package ready for Deliver?** Build doesn't brief the team; that's Deliver's first job. Build produces the list Deliver briefs from: every person whose handoff changes when this goes live, and what changes for them. Without that list, Deliver starts blind.

Yes to all five and Build is done. No to any one of them and you fix what failed, run the test again, and don't advance on a partial pass.

Meridian's build passed on real RFQs from the prior two weeks. Elena assembled most of the workflow herself; the freelancer came in only for the API wiring the spec had budgeted. The pricing spreadsheet took more work than anything else: expired discounts and contradictory terms, 147 rows cut to 112 validated rules by hand. What she handed Deliver was the three projects the spec named, Quote Research, Quote Pricing, and Quote Assembly, drafting every quote, with her reviewing each one before Ty sends it.

A system that runs isn't yet a system the business has absorbed. That's the next chapter's work.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Pull last week's real inputs and run the full five-question Done Test. Write down the results, fix what failed, retest. Those results go into the handoff to Deliver.
:::

## Reflect on your operation

1. Take your Sprint's designed workflow and pick the product it runs on: Claude Projects, Claude Team, Claude Code, a low-code platform, or a server of your own. Does that match where your team assumed you'd end up? If not, which assumption was wrong?
2. Answer the seven guardrails questions for your workflow right now. Which one is hardest? Is that difficulty telling you Design needs another session, or that you genuinely haven't decided yet?
3. Who in your company is closest to the constraint you're solving, and what would they have to learn to build the workflow themselves? Name the person, name the gap. If your answer is "we'd hand it to a developer," ask what the waiting costs you.
4. Open your spec and read Section 7 out loud. If you can't say what the workflow does when a system it depends on is down, you have a design gap, not a build task.

Deliver is where the deployed system gets put in front of real work, and where the number you wrote down in Signal gets measured.
